unit.title: How attacks work, and how to defend

lesson.title: Attacks on passwords, and the defences
lesson.subtitle: Guessing, leaks and reuse, and why long and unique wins

video.title: Attacks on passwords, and the defences
video.format_note: Animated explainer for students aged 12–16, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Mr Joseph Mwangi — computer studies teacher (main character)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, talking to the student)

scenes.visual: Mr Joseph at his desk, a student's phone in front of him showing a locked social media profile. Behind him, a faded forum logo with a crack through it.
scenes.animation: The forum logo cracks; a line runs from it to the phone.
scenes.narration: “I used the same password everywhere, but it was a strong one!” A student told me that after her account was taken over. A small gaming forum she’d joined years ago had been hacked. Her strong password was in the leak, and someone tried it everywhere.

scenes.visual: Paper-grey card: the Darsi mark, the lesson title and the cyber track chip.
scenes.animation: Mark pops in; title slides up.
scenes.on_screen_text: Attacks on passwords, and the defences
scenes.narration: Today: how attackers get passwords, and the defences that stop them.

scenes.visual: Four rows with icons: a short list, a book of words, a spinning counter, a leaked file.
scenes.animation: Rows slide in as each way is named.
scenes.narration: Attackers get passwords in four main ways. They guess the common ones: one two three four five six, names, birthdays, football teams. They try long lists of words. They try every possible combination. And they reuse passwords from leaks.

scenes.visual: Left: a website login with a timer after wrong tries. Right: a stolen file on the attacker's own computer, a fast counter spinning.
scenes.animation: The left timer ticks slowly; the right counter blurs.
scenes.on_screen_text: A website is slow; a leak is fast
scenes.narration: Guessing on a website is slow. After a few wrong tries, a good site makes you wait or locks the account. The real danger is a leak: when a site’s password file is stolen, attackers can guess on their own computers, with no limit.

scenes.visual: Two columns: eight letter tiles with a stopwatch reading seconds; five word tiles with a calendar counting years.
scenes.animation: Numbers count up in each column.
scenes.narration: Here’s where length matters. Eight random lower-case letters give about two hundred billion possibilities. A gaming computer guessing ten billion a second tries them all in about twenty seconds. Five random words would take the same computer about ninety years.

scenes.visual: A bicycle lock with number wheels. A wheel is added, then another; the count of combinations jumps each time. Then a wheel with thousands of words instead of digits.
scenes.animation: Wheels click into place one by one.
scenes.narration: Think of a bicycle lock with number wheels. Each extra wheel multiplies the combinations by ten. A random word is like a wheel with thousands of positions.

scenes.visual: Ms Salma at the board with three password cards pinned up. Three answer cards drop in.
scenes.animation: Salma slides in; the cards drop with a small bounce.
scenes.narration: Quick check! A site’s password file leaks. Which lasts longest: a name and a birth year, eight random letters, or five random words?

scenes.visual: The ‘five random words’ card gets a check badge; the other two crumble.
scenes.animation: Check badge pops; the two cards fall away.
scenes.narration: Five random words. Names and birth years are tried first, so they fall almost at once. Eight random letters sound strong, but a fast computer gets through them in seconds.

scenes.visual: One leaked file in the middle; arrows fan out to many app icons: email, chat, a game, a shop. Each one lights up red.
scenes.animation: Arrows shoot out; icons turn red one after another.
scenes.narration: Now one of the most common attacks: reuse. Attackers take the emails and passwords from one leak and try them on hundreds of other sites, automatically. It’s called credential stuffing. If you used the same password, every account falls together, however strong it was.

scenes.visual: A website drawn as a building with three guards: a lock with a timer, a fingerprint card, a list being checked.
scenes.animation: Each guard steps forward as it is named.
scenes.narration: Good websites defend you too. They slow down or lock after too many wrong tries. They store a fingerprint of your password, not the password itself. And they check new passwords against lists of leaked ones.

scenes.visual: Three numbered steps: a row of random-word tiles, a vault with many keys, a phone showing a code.
scenes.narration: Your part is simple. Use a long passphrase of random words. Use a different one for every account, and let a password manager remember them. Turn on two-step sign-in, so a leaked password alone isn’t enough.

scenes.visual: Mr Joseph holds up an old game controller and an email icon joined by the same key. Two answer cards bounce in.
scenes.animation: Cards bounce in one by one.
scenes.narration: Your turn. A gaming site you used years ago was hacked, and you used the same password for your email. Why does that matter?

scenes.visual: The ‘attackers try it on your email’ card gets the check badge. Three summary cards line up: word tiles, separate keys, a phone with a code.
scenes.animation: Cards line up left to right.
scenes.narration: Because attackers try every leaked password on other sites, your email included. So change it now, everywhere you used it. Remember: long random words, one password per account, and two-step sign-in.

scenes.visual: A student writes a list of app names in a notebook, no passwords, and circles two that share a key. End card: the Darsi mark.
scenes.animation: Circles draw around two names; end card fades in.
scenes.narration: Try it tomorrow: list your accounts on paper, with no passwords on it. Mark every place you used the same password, and change those first, starting with your email.

checkpoints.prompt: A site’s password file leaks. Which password lasts longest?

options.text: A name and a birth year, like Amira2011!

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — each random word multiplies the possibilities by thousands. Names and years are tried first, and 8 letters fall in seconds.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — names and years are among the first guesses, and 8 random letters fall in seconds to a fast computer. Five random words would take about 90 years.

checkpoints.prompt: A gaming site you used years ago was hacked. You used the same password for your email. Why does it matter?

options.text: It doesn’t — the gaming site is a different company
Attackers try the leaked password on your email too

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — leaked passwords are tried on many other sites automatically. Change it everywhere you used it.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — it’s a different company, but attackers try leaked passwords on other sites automatically. Change it everywhere you used it.
